  routine was a stubborn anchor. For twenty-four years, the lantern had not faltered on his watch, and tonight, with the barometer plummeting
  and the Atlantic heaving against the granite foundations, failure was not an option.

  He reached the lantern room, where the damp cold of the ocean gave way to the sharp, comforting aromas of whale oil, brass polish, and
  paraffin. Outside, a gale whipped sheets of spray against the curved storm panes, rattling the iron frame with frantic, shuddering gusts.
  Arthur checked the brass clockwork mechanism that rotated the great Fresnel lens. He caught the heavy counterweight rope, hauling it upward
  hand over hand until the iron cylinder clicked securely against its ceiling stop. With a calibrated nudge, he engaged the escapement,
  setting the concentric rings of prismatic glass into their steady, hypnotic rotation.

  Striking a long wooden match against the wall, Arthur shielded the sulfur flame with a calloused palm and touched it to the primary burner.
  The wick caught, guttered briefly, and then flared into brilliant gold. Instantly, the faceted lenses seized the flame, bending and
  magnifying its modest radiance into three blazing spears that pierced the gloom, sweeping over the roiling surf every fifteen seconds.

  Arthur settled onto his high wooden stool by the logbook. Below, black rollers smashed against the jagged spine of Devil’s Tooth, throwing
  plumes of spectral froth fifty feet into the night. It was an unforgiving coast, littered with the ribs of forgotten schooners. Through his
  brass spyglass, he scanned the squall-choked horizon. There, barely visible between the swells three miles south, flickered the faint green
  running light of an outbound freighter.

  He watched in silence as the ship altered course by five degrees, aligning itself cleanly with the safe channel marked by his sweeping
  beacon. The light touched the drenched hull once, twice, and then the vessel slipped safely away toward open water. Outside, the storm
  continued to howl, but inside the glass crown, the mechanical pulse beat on without haste. Arthur dipped his steel nib into dark ink and
  recorded the hour, the squall's bearing, and the solitary passage, deeply content in the purposeful quiet of his vigil.
